   427→
   428→## Recommended Phase Structure
   429→
   430→This is the critical content decision (within Claude's discretion): how to structure 5-6 phases. The following five-phase structure is recommended, grounded in the architecture research and locked decisions.
   431→
   432→### Phase 0: Hardware and Environment Validation
   433→
   434→**Goal:** Confirm the hardware and software environment is ready for GPU-dependent work. This is a precondition gate, not a research gate.
   435→
   436→**Key deliverables:**
   437→- Both RTX 4090 GPUs recognized by CUDA (both in `nvidia-smi` output, both accessible via `torch.cuda.device_count()`)
   438→- PyTorch nightly cu128 forward+backward pass completes without segfault on both GPUs
   439→- vLLM serves Qwen2.5-Coder-7B with `--pipeline-parallel-size 2 --tensor-parallel-size 1` without crash
   440→- vLLM serves a known-good adapter and produces correct output (regression test to confirm TP+LoRA corruption is absent)
   441→- PEFT + bitsandbytes QLoRA fine-tune runs 1 training step without error
   442→
   443→**Hardware constraints to document explicitly (per README.md):**
   444→- Hardware: dual RTX 4090 (Ada Lovelace, sm_89), 24 GB VRAM each, 48 GB total, CXL interconnect
   445→- `--pipeline-parallel-size 2, --tensor-parallel-size 1` — required; TP+LoRA is a confirmed vLLM bug (#21471), not architecture-specific
   446→- PCIe bottleneck: RTX 4090 lacks NVLink; all-reduce over PCIe is prohibitive; pipeline parallelism passes only activations at layer boundaries
   447→- PyTorch: nightly cu128 (project choice per README, even though Ada/sm_89 is supported by stable PyTorch)
   448→- CUDA: 12.8+ (cu128)
   449→
   450→**Success criteria style:** Binary pass/fail checklist. No metrics.
   451→
   452→### Phase 1: Core Hypothesis Validation (Kill-Switch Gate)
   453→
   454→**Goal:** Determine empirically whether the Doc-to-LoRA approach can encode coding trajectories into useful LoRA adapters. No infrastructure is built until this passes.
   455→
   456→**Key deliverables:**
   457→- Minimal Doc-to-LoRA hypernetwork trained on 50-100 coding trajectory pairs
   458→- Adapter quality evaluation on held-out HumanEval tasks (not full HumanEval — a held-out subset of 20-30 tasks)
   459→- MLflow run documenting: Pass@1 vs baseline, training loss curve, adapter cosine diversity, ||ΔW|| norms
   460→- Written assessment: what passed, what failed, what was learned
   461→
   462→**Hardware note:** Run the baseline in bfloat16 (not QLoRA) to isolate the hypothesis from quantization artifacts. QLoRA is introduced in Phase 2 after the baseline passes. This isolates the two variables: (1) does the hypernetwork approach work? (2) does quantization degrade it?
   463→
   464→**Experiment sketch:**
   465→- Dataset: 50-100 real coding trajectory pairs from HumanEval or SWE-bench-lite; each trajectory = (task description, attempt sequence, final passing code)
   466→- Baseline: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct with no adapter (raw model Pass@1)
   467→- Eval method: Pass@1 on a 20-30 task held-out subset of HumanEval; run 5 samples per task
   468→- Expected range: 5-15% improvement over baseline signals a real effect; < 5% improvement = gate fails
   469→
   470→**Kill-switch:** If Pass@1 improvement < 5% on held-out tasks, the project stops and reassesses. No predefined fallback. The failure is documented as a research finding.
   471→
   472→**Secondary diagnostic signals** (tracked via MLflow, not gating criteria):
   473→- Adapter cosine diversity > 0.1 across training batch (detecting mode collapse early)
   474→- Training loss converges and does not plateau in first 5% of budget
   475→- ||ΔW|| is meaningfully nonzero (adapter is not being ignored by the base model)
   476→
   477→### Phase 2: Adapter Library and Serving Infrastructure
   478→
   479→**Goal:** Build the component foundation that all subsequent phases depend on: the adapter registry, the vLLM server with dynamic LoRA loading, and the API service extensions.
   480→
   481→**Key deliverables:**
   482→- `libs/adapter-registry`: SQLModel schema, write-once enforcement, path resolution for `.safetensors` files
   483→- `services/lora-server`: vLLM Dockerfile, startup script (PP=2, TP=1, enable-lora), basic health check
   484→- `services/api-service` extensions: `/adapters` and `/sessions` routes; SQLModel tables
   485→- QLoRA integration: bfloat16 baseline → NF4 QLoRA transition with quality comparison logged to MLflow
   486→
   487→**Primary risk callout — Adapter composition interference:** Default must be single-adapter-per-request at inference time. Multi-adapter composition is an optional future experiment, not the default. Direct additive merging of heterogeneous LoRAs produces interference in non-orthogonal subspaces.
   488→
   489→**Primary risk callout — Catastrophic forgetting:** The adapter registry must enforce write-once semantics at the storage API level. No code path may overwrite an existing adapter. Adapters are immutable, indexed by session ID and timestamp.
   490→
   491→**Success criteria:** Mix of checklists (adapter registry stores/retrieves correctly; vLLM server starts and serves with dynamic LoRA loading; no TP=2 flag anywhere in config) and metrics (QLoRA quality vs bfloat16 baseline < 10% degradation on held-out HumanEval tasks; logged in MLflow).
   492→
   493→### Phase 3: Recursive Agent Loop and Sandbox Integration
   494→
   495→**Goal:** Build the core agent loop (`services/rune-agent`) and the sandboxed code execution environment. This phase produces the first end-to-end path from task to adapter.
   496→
   497→**Key deliverables:**
   498→- `services/rune-agent`: LangGraph StateGraph with `generate → execute → reflect → save` cycle
   499→- Sandbox integration: Docker-based code execution with network isolation, memory/CPU limits
   500→- Adapter selection: query adapter-registry at session start, load most-relevant adapter into lora-server
   501→- End-to-end test: task → agent loop → successful code → trajectory captured → passed to distillation
   502→- `libs/model-training` extensions: PEFT utilities, trajectory-to-adapter fine-tuning script
   503→
   504→**Success criteria:** Checklists. Binary pass/fail for each integration point. No metrics in this phase — the agent loop producing valid adapters is the success.
   505→
   506→### Phase 4: Evolution Operator and Hypernetwork
   507→
   508→**Goal:** Build the adapter lifecycle management system (`services/evolution-svc`) and the Doc-to-LoRA hypernetwork inference path (`services/training-svc` hypernetwork job). This is the final phase and depends on having a corpus of adapters produced by Phase 3.
   509→
   510→**Key deliverables:**
   511→- `services/evolution-svc`: fitness evaluation, tournament selection, pruning, adapter promotion
   512→- `services/training-svc`: hypernetwork training job; hypernetwork inference (single forward pass → adapter)
   513→- Adapter hierarchy: project-root, domain, task-specific levels populated by evolution
   514→- MLflow tracking: adapter fitness scores, evolution events, hypernetwork reconstruction loss
   515→
   516→**Primary risk callout — Hypernetwork mode collapse:** Diversity regularization must be in the training loss from the start. Monitor adapter cosine diversity metric — if it falls below threshold, training stops. The degenerate solution (mean adapter) has near-zero variance across different inputs.
   517→
   518→**Primary risk callout — Minimum corpus size:** The hypernetwork requires a diverse corpus of pre-trained adapters. If Phase 3 has not produced at least 50-100 diverse task-adapter pairs, delay hypernetwork training and continue accumulating adapters.
   519→
   520→**Success criteria:** Mix of metrics (hypernetwork reconstruction loss on held-out adapters; adapter cosine diversity > threshold) and checklists (evolution operator promotes, prunes, and archives adapters without corrupting the registry; hypernetwork produces adapters that load and run without error in vLLM).
   521→
   522→---
   523→
   524→## State of the Art
   525→
   526→| Old Approach | Current Approach | When Changed | Impact for This Plan |
   527→|--------------|------------------|--------------|---------------------|
   528→| All phases presented as equally certain | Phase 1 as explicit kill-switch gate | Research project management best practice | Plan explicitly stops at Phase 1 if hypothesis fails |
   529→| Time-boxed phases | Dependency-ordered phases, no time estimates | User decision for this project | Phases are contingent, not scheduled |
   530→| Infrastructure first, hypothesis second | Hypothesis first, infrastructure contingent | Learned from failed ML projects (RAND 2024 research) | Adapter registry and agent loop are only built if Phase 1 passes |
   531→| Tensor parallelism for multi-GPU | Pipeline parallelism (PP=2, TP=1) | vLLM issue #21471, applies to RTX 4090 + all consumer GPUs | Plan mandates PP=2 in all phases that reference multi-GPU serving |
   532→| bfloat16 throughout | bfloat16 for baseline, QLoRA introduced after hypothesis validates | QLoRA paper recommendation; isolate variables | Phase 1 runs in bfloat16; Phase 2 introduces QLoRA with explicit comparison |
   533→
   534→---
   535→
   536→## Open Questions
   537→
   538→1. **MkDocs theme: keep default or upgrade to Material?**
   539→   - What we know: Current config uses `theme: name: mkdocs` (default MkDocs theme)
   540→   - What's unclear: Whether to upgrade to Material for MkDocs (richer features, admonitions, better nav)
   541→   - Recommendation: Keep the default theme. The user decision is to use MkDocs natively without adding a new framework. Material is a separate install and a separate decision.
   542→
   543→2. **Exact HumanEval subset size for Phase 1 kill-switch evaluation**
   544→   - What we know: HumanEval has 164 tasks; 5% Pass@1 improvement is the threshold; the plan says "held-out subset"
   545→   - What's unclear: How many tasks constitute a statistically meaningful held-out subset for the kill-switch decision
   546→   - Recommendation: Use 20-30 tasks as the held-out subset. At 5 samples per task this is 100-150 evaluations — sufficient for a directional result without being a full benchmark run. This is within Claude's discretion.
   547→
   548→3. **MkDocs docs_dir — keep `docs/` or create `docs/rune/`?**
   549→   - What we know: Current config: `docs_dir: docs`; files go in `docs/`
   550→   - What's unclear: Whether to create a subdirectory to separate Rune docs from template remnants
   551→   - Recommendation: Use the existing `docs/` directory. Create `docs/appendices/` as a new subdirectory for the appendix files. Replace template files (index.md) in-place. Keep the directory structure flat.
   552→
   553→4. **How to handle existing docs files (onboarding.md, testing-guide.md, components-overview.md)**
   554→   - What we know: These are template content, not Rune content. User decision: remove template placeholder docs.
   555→   - What's unclear: Whether to delete the files or just remove them from the nav
   556→   - Recommendation: Remove from the nav only — do not delete the files. MkDocs does not complain about files in docs_dir that are not in the nav (only warns via `omitted_files: warn`). The nav controls what is published; the files can remain as orphans. This is safer than deletion.
   557→
   558→5. **site_url in mkdocs.yml**
   559→   - What we know: Current value is `https://elixirtrials-.github.io/template-repo/docs/` — clearly template placeholder
   560→   - What's unclear: Whether GitHub Pages will be used; what the correct URL should be
   561→   - Recommendation: Update site_url to the actual GitHub repository URL, or remove the field if not publishing to GitHub Pages. This does not affect local `mkdocs serve`.
   562→

   121→Brief intro paragraph (2-3 sentences): This appendix enumerates the primary research risks identified during architecture research. Each risk is assigned to the implementation phase where it is most relevant and where its mitigation is tested. Risks are ordered by severity.

   125→Include these three risks (from PITFALLS.md research, confirmed in ROADMAP.md):

   127→1. **Hypernetwork mode collapse** — Phase 1 (kill-switch) and Phase 4 — Severity: High — Mitigation: Diversity regularization in training loss from the start; monitor adapter cosine diversity metric (> 0.1 threshold); the degenerate solution (mean adapter) has near-zero variance across different inputs — Warning signs: Generated adapters cluster tightly in PCA; cosine similarity between adapters approaches 1.0; training loss converges but Pass@1 does not improve.
   128→
   129→2. **Adapter composition interference** — Phase 2 — Severity: Medium — Mitigation: Default to single-adapter retrieval at inference time; treat multi-adapter composition as an optional future experiment; direct additive merging of heterogeneous LoRAs produces interference in non-orthogonal subspaces — Warning signs: Performance with 2 adapters loaded is worse than 1; inference latency increases non-linearly with adapter count.
   130→
   131→3. **Catastrophic forgetting** — Phase 2 — Severity: Medium — Mitigation: Immutable adapter storage with write-once semantics enforced at the registry API level; no code path may overwrite an existing adapter; adapters indexed by session ID and timestamp — Warning signs: Performance on session-1 tasks degrades after session-50 adapters are added to the corpus; adapter file checksums change unexpectedly.

   270→# Rune Implementation Plan
   271→
   272→## Executive Summary
   273→- Goal: 1-2 sentences stating what the plan achieves
   274→- Phase overview table: | Phase | Goal | Gate |
   275→  (5 rows for Phase 0-4; Phase 1 marked as kill-switch)
   276→- Key risks: 3 bullets naming the three research risks (link to risk matrix appendix)

   278→- Mermaid dependency graph: flowchart TD showing Phase 0 → Phase 1 (diamond, kill-switch) → Phase 2 → Phase 3 → Phase 4, with a "Stop and Reassess" path from Phase 1 failure
   279→- Framing note: 1 paragraph establishing that this is a research-stage plan, phases after the gate are contingent
   280→
   281→## Phase 0: Hardware and Environment Validation
   282→- **Depends on:** Nothing (first phase)
   283→- Goal paragraph: confirm hardware/software environment before GPU-dependent work
   284→- Why this phase comes first: 1-2 paragraphs (cannot do anything GPU-related without confirmed environment)
   285→- Deliverables checklist:
   286→  - [ ] Both RTX 4090 GPUs recognized by CUDA (`nvidia-smi`, `torch.cuda.device_count() == 2`)
   287→  - [ ] PyTorch nightly cu128 forward+backward pass completes without segfault on both GPUs
   288→  - [ ] vLLM serves Qwen2.5-Coder-7B with `--pipeline-parallel-size 2 --tensor-parallel-size 1` without crash
   289→  - [ ] vLLM serves a known-good LoRA adapter and produces correct output (confirming TP+LoRA corruption absent under PP=2)
   290→  - [ ] PEFT + bitsandbytes QLoRA fine-tune runs 1 training step without error (confirming quantization toolchain)
   291→- Hardware constraints: document explicitly — dual RTX 4090, Ada Lovelace (sm_89), 24 GB each, CXL, PP=2 mandate, PCIe bottleneck (no NVLink), PyTorch nightly cu128, CUDA 12.8+
   292→- Risk callouts: driver/CUDA version mismatch, vLLM build from source may be needed for PP=2 support
   293→- Success criteria table: all binary pass/fail, no metrics
   294→- No experiment sketch (this is a validation gate, not a research phase)
   295→
   296→## Phase 1: Core Hypothesis Validation (Kill-Switch Gate)
   297→- **Depends on:** Phase 0 passes all success criteria
   298→- Goal paragraph: determine empirically whether Doc-to-LoRA encodes coding trajectories into useful LoRA adapters. No infrastructure is built until this passes.
   299→- Why this phase comes here: 1-2 paragraphs (hypothesis-first, infrastructure-contingent; cite RAND 2024 pattern of failed ML projects that built infrastructure before validating the core idea)
   300→- Deliverables checklist:
   301→  - [ ] Minimal Doc-to-LoRA hypernetwork trained on 50-100 coding trajectory pairs
   302→  - [ ] Adapter quality evaluation on held-out HumanEval subset (20-30 tasks)
   303→  - [ ] MLflow run documenting: Pass@1 vs baseline, training loss curve, adapter cosine diversity, ||delta-W|| norms
   304→  - [ ] Written assessment: what passed, what failed, what was learned
   305→- **Kill-switch** section (visually distinct — use blockquote or admonition):
   306→  - Primary metric: >= 5% Pass@1 improvement on held-out HumanEval tasks over Qwen2.5-Coder-7B baseline
   307→  - If gate fails: stop and document what was learned. No predefined fallback. The failure itself narrows the design space.
   308→  - What passing means: proceed to Phase 2. The hypothesis has empirical support (not proof — support).
   309→- Secondary diagnostic signals (tracked via MLflow, NOT gating criteria):
   310→  - Adapter cosine diversity > 0.1 across training batch (detecting mode collapse early)
   311→  - Training loss converges and does not plateau in first 5% of budget
   312→  - ||delta-W|| is meaningfully nonzero (adapter is not ignored by the base model)
   313→- Hardware note: Run baseline in bfloat16 (NOT QLoRA) to isolate hypothesis from quantization artifacts. QLoRA introduced in Phase 2 after baseline passes.
   314→- Risk callouts: hypernetwork mode collapse (link to risk matrix); training data quality (trajectories must be diverse, not repetitive)
   315→- Success criteria table: primary metric (5% Pass@1) + binary checklists
   316→- Experiment sketch (~5-7 lines):
   317→  - Dataset: 50-100 real coding trajectory pairs from HumanEval or SWE-bench-lite
   318→  - Baseline: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct with no adapter (raw model Pass@1)
   319→  - Eval method: Pass@1 on 20-30 task held-out subset; 5 samples per task
   320→  - Expected range: 5-15% improvement signals real effect; < 5% = gate fails
   321→  - Tracking: MLflow experiment with run_id, phase, adapter_id, pass_at_1, training_loss, adapter_cosine_diversity
   322→
   323→## Phase 2: Adapter Library and Serving Infrastructure
   324→- **Depends on:** Phase 1 kill-switch passes
   325→- Goal paragraph: build the component foundation — adapter registry, vLLM server with dynamic LoRA, API service extensions, QLoRA integration
   326→- Why this phase comes here: 1-2 paragraphs (adapter registry is the dependency root of the build order; serving infrastructure unblocks all subsequent phases)
   327→- Deliverables checklist:
   328→  - [ ] libs/adapter-registry: SQLModel schema, write-once enforcement, .safetensors path resolution
   329→  - [ ] services/lora-server: vLLM Dockerfile, PP=2/TP=1 startup, dynamic LoRA loading, health check
   330→  - [ ] services/api-service extensions: /adapters and /sessions routes, SQLModel tables
   331→  - [ ] QLoRA integration: bfloat16 baseline to NF4 QLoRA transition with quality comparison logged to MLflow
   332→- Risk callouts: adapter composition interference, catastrophic forgetting (link to risk matrix)
   333→- Success criteria table: mix of checklists and metrics (QLoRA vs bfloat16 < 10% degradation on held-out HumanEval)

   339→- Why this phase comes here: 1-2 paragraphs (requires adapter registry and serving from Phase 2; produces the adapter corpus needed for Phase 4)
   340→- Deliverables checklist:

     1→# Roadmap: Rune — v1.0 Documentation & Implementation Plan
     2→
     3→## Overview
     4→
     5→Three phases of documentation work that transform the Rune architecture specification into communicable artifacts: a public-facing README, a phased engineering plan grounded in hardware reality and research risk, and internal architecture documentation covering the recursive loop, component mapping, and multi-GPU strategy. All phases produce Markdown files, not code. Phase 2 depends on Phase 1 (implementation plan references the README framing), and Phase 3 depends on Phase 2 (architecture docs reference the build order from the plan).
     6→
     7→## Phases
     8→
     9→**Phase Numbering:**
    10→- Integer phases (1, 2, 3): Planned milestone work
    11→- Decimal phases (2.1, 2.2): Urgent insertions (marked with INSERTED)
    12→
    13→Decimal phases appear between their surrounding integers in numeric order.
    14→
    15→- [x] **Phase 1: README** - Write the project README covering vision, architecture overview, hardware requirements, current status, and paper references (completed 2026-03-02)
    16→- [ ] **Phase 2: Implementation Plan** - Write the phased implementation plan with hardware/environment validation, kill-switch feasibility gate, risk-addressed phases, and build order
    17→- [ ] **Phase 3: Architecture Docs** - Write architecture documentation covering the recursive loop, monorepo component mapping, adapter storage, and multi-GPU strategy
    18→
    19→## Phase Details
    20→
    21→### Phase 1: README
    22→**Goal**: A polished README.md exists that anyone can read to understand what Rune is, how it works, what hardware it needs, where the project stands, and which papers it builds on
    23→**Depends on**: Nothing (first phase)
    24→**Requirements**: DOC-01, DOC-02, DOC-03, DOC-04, DOC-05
    25→**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):
    26→  1. A reader new to Rune can explain the core innovation (parametric episodic memory via LoRA) and how it differs from Aider, Cursor, and Claude Code after reading the README
    27→  2. The architecture overview section describes the recursive loop, hypernetwork, evolution operator, and adapter serving — with a diagram or structured visual representation of data flow
    28→  3. The hardware requirements section lists specific prerequisites (dual RTX 4090, CUDA 12.8+, PyTorch nightly cu128, QLoRA) so a developer knows before cloning whether they can run Rune
    29→  4. The current status section honestly states that no implementation exists, this is a research-stage project, and the core hypothesis (Doc-to-LoRA on coding trajectories) is unvalidated
    30→  5. The references section cites Doc-to-LoRA (arXiv:2602.15902), S-LoRA (arXiv:2311.03285), and QLoRA (arXiv:2305.14314) with links
    31→**Plans:** 1/1 plans complete
    32→Plans:
    33→- [x] 01-01-PLAN.md — Write complete README.md (vision, architecture diagrams, hardware, status, references)
    34→
    35→### Phase 2: Implementation Plan
    36→**Goal**: A detailed, phased implementation plan document exists that transforms the Rune architecture specification into actionable phases with pass/fail criteria, risk gates, and a concrete build order grounded in hardware reality
    37→**Depends on**: Phase 1
    38→**Requirements**: PLAN-01, PLAN-02, PLAN-03, PLAN-04, PLAN-05, PLAN-06
    39→**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):
    40→  1. Phase 0 of the implementation plan defines hardware and environment validation with specific pass/fail criteria (both GPUs recognized, PyTorch nightly cu128 forward+backward pass without segfault, vLLM serving Qwen2.5-Coder-7B via pipeline parallelism without TP+LoRA corruption)
    41→  2. Phase 1 of the implementation plan is structured as a kill-switch gate: it defines a measurable success threshold (at minimum, 5% Pass@1 improvement on held-out HumanEval tasks) and states explicitly that no infrastructure is built if this gate fails
    42→  3. Every subsequent phase in the plan states its deliverables, which previous phase it depends on, and the success criteria that mark it complete
    43→  4. The plan explicitly addresses the three primary research risks: adapter composition interference (heterogeneous subspaces), hypernetwork mode collapse (mean-adapter collapse), and catastrophic forgetting (non-immutable adapter writes) — each with a mitigation strategy
    44→  5. The plan reflects the hardware reality: dual RTX 4090 with CXL, pipeline parallelism (PP=2) not tensor parallelism, QLoRA as required for 24GB per-GPU constraint, with QLoRA introduced only after Phase 1 bfloat16 baseline passes
    45→  6. The plan includes the recommended build order: adapter-registry → lora-server → model-training extensions → api-service extensions → rune-agent → evolution-svc → training-svc → hypernetwork
    46→**Plans:** 2 plans
    47→Plans:
    48→- [ ] 02-01-PLAN.md — Clean MkDocs config, replace landing page, write risk matrix and build order appendices
    49→- [ ] 02-02-PLAN.md — Write main implementation plan document (5 phases, kill-switch gate, executive summary)
    50→
    51→### Phase 3: Architecture Docs
    52→**Goal**: Internal architecture documentation exists covering the four core design decisions that implementation will depend on: the recursive code generation loop, how Rune maps to the existing monorepo, the adapter storage strategy, and the multi-GPU inference and training strategy
    53→**Depends on**: Phase 2
    54→**Requirements**: ARCH-01, ARCH-02, ARCH-03, ARCH-04
    55→**Success Criteria** (what must be TRUE):
    56→  1. The recursive code generation loop document shows explicit data flow: what enters each step (generate, execute, reflect, distill), what exits, what triggers a retry, and what terminates the loop
    57→  2. The monorepo mapping document lists each new Rune service (rune-agent, lora-server, training-svc, evolution-svc, adapter-registry) alongside the existing monorepo service it extends or runs alongside, with integration points named

     1→# Rune
     2→
     3→## What This Is
     4→
     5→Rune is a local-first coding agent that uses LoRA weight space as episodic memory, enabling unbounded context for Small Language Models (<10B params). Instead of stuffing tokens into context windows, Rune encodes procedural knowledge—architecture specs, execution feedback, coding conventions—directly into composable LoRA adapters via a Doc-to-LoRA hypernetwork. Each coding session produces reusable adapters that persist across sessions and compose hierarchically.
     6→
     7→## Core Value
     8→
     9→A local coding agent that learns from its own coding trajectories, building persistent parametric memory that scales independently of context window size.

     1→# Rune Implementation Plan
     2→
     3→## Executive Summary
     4→
     5→Rune proposes to validate and implement a system that encodes coding trajectories into LoRA adapters using a Doc-to-LoRA hypernetwork, accumulating parametric memory that persists across sessions. This plan covers the full journey from hardware validation through hypernetwork training across five implementation phases (Phase 0 through Phase 4), structured so that the core hypothesis is validated before infrastructure is built.
     6→
     7→### Phase Overview
     8→
     9→| Phase | Goal | Gate |
    10→|-------|------|------|
    11→| Phase 0 | Hardware and environment validation | Precondition (all binary pass/fail) |
    12→| Phase 1 | Core hypothesis validation — Doc-to-LoRA on coding tasks | **Kill-switch** (5% Pass@1 threshold) |
    13→| Phase 2 | Adapter library and serving infrastructure | Success criteria (checklist + metrics) |
    14→| Phase 3 | Recursive agent loop and sandbox integration | Success criteria (checklists) |
    15→| Phase 4 | Evolution operator and hypernetwork | Success criteria (metrics + checklists) |
    16→
    17→### Key Risks
    18→
    19→Three primary research risks are tracked throughout this plan. See [Risk Matrix](appendices/risk-matrix.md) for full mitigation strategies and warning signs.
    20→
    21→- **Hypernetwork mode collapse** — The degenerate solution (mean adapter) has near-zero variance across inputs; diversity regularization in the training loss is required from the start.
    22→- **Adapter composition interference** — Direct additive merging of heterogeneous LoRAs produces interference in non-orthogonal subspaces; default to single-adapter retrieval.
    23→- **Catastrophic forgetting** — Adapter registry must enforce write-once semantics; no code path may overwrite an existing adapter.
    24→
    25→### Build Order
    26→
    27→The recommended component build sequence is detailed in [Build Order](appendices/build-order.md). The dependency root is `libs/adapter-registry` — it must be built first, as all other components depend on it for adapter storage and retrieval.
    28→
    29→### Phase Dependency Graph
    30→
    31→```mermaid
    32→flowchart TD
    33→    P0[Phase 0\nHardware Validation] --> P1
    34→    P1{Phase 1\nHypothesis Gate} -->|passes| P2
    35→    P1 -->|fails| Stop([Stop and Reassess])
    36→    P2[Phase 2\nAdapter Library\n+ Serving] --> P3
    37→    P3[Phase 3\nRecursive Agent\nLoop] --> P4
    38→    P4[Phase 4\nEvolution Operator\n+ Hypernetwork]
    39→```
    40→
    41→### Research-Stage Framing
    42→
    43→This plan is structured for a research-stage system: the phases after the kill-switch gate (Phase 2 through Phase 4) are contingent on the hypothesis validated in Phase 1. Writing them out does not imply confidence that they will be reached — it means the design is complete enough to proceed if the hypothesis holds. If Phase 1 fails, the plan does not prescribe a pivot. The failure itself is informative and narrows the design space.
    44→
    45→---
    46→
    47→## Phase 0: Hardware and Environment Validation
    48→
    49→**Depends on:** Nothing — this is the first phase.
    50→
    51→Phase 0 confirms that the hardware and software environment is ready for GPU-dependent work. This is a precondition gate, not a research gate: none of the hypothesis testing in Phase 1 is possible without a validated environment. The success criteria are entirely binary — each check either passes or fails, with no partial credit.
    52→
    53→### Why This Phase Comes First
    54→
    55→GPU-dependent workloads fail in hardware-specific, non-obvious ways: CUDA version mismatches cause segfaults during backward passes, vLLM may require compilation from source for newer pipeline-parallelism features, and the TP+LoRA corruption bug (vLLM issue #21471) can produce silently wrong outputs rather than crashes. Discovering any of these mid-experiment invalidates results and forces a debugging detour. Phase 0 establishes a clean baseline before any research work begins.
    56→
    57→The distinction between Phase 0 and an installation guide is intentional. Phase 0 validates that the environment works correctly — the pass/fail tests confirm behavior, not installation. The steps required to achieve a passing environment (installing drivers, compiling vLLM, configuring CUDA paths) are pre-conditions that precede this phase.
    58→
    59→### Hardware Constraints
    60→
    61→| Component | Specification |
    62→|-----------|---------------|
    63→| GPU | 2x NVIDIA RTX 4090 (Ada Lovelace, sm_89), 24 GB VRAM each, 48 GB total |
    64→| GPU Interconnect | CXL (cache-coherent memory pooling) |
    65→| Multi-GPU Strategy | Pipeline parallelism: `--pipeline-parallel-size 2 --tensor-parallel-size 1` |
    66→| CUDA | 12.8+ (cu128) |
    67→| PyTorch | 2.9+ (nightly, cu128 wheels) |
    68→| Quantization toolchain | PEFT + bitsandbytes (QLoRA, NF4 4-bit) |
    69→
    70→**Note on tensor parallelism:** `--tensor-parallel-size 2` is explicitly excluded. All-reduce operations over PCIe (~32 GB/s) are prohibitively expensive compared to NVLink (~112 GB/s per direction). Pipeline parallelism passes activations only at layer boundaries and is the correct strategy for this interconnect. The TP+LoRA corruption bug (vLLM #21471) applies to this hardware configuration and is confirmed absent under PP=2.
    71→
    72→### Deliverables
    73→
    74→- [ ] Both RTX 4090 GPUs recognized by CUDA (`nvidia-smi` lists both; `torch.cuda.device_count() == 2`)
    75→- [ ] PyTorch nightly cu128 forward pass and backward pass complete without segfault on both GPUs
    76→- [ ] vLLM serves Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct with `--pipeline-parallel-size 2 --tensor-parallel-size 1` without crash
    77→- [ ] vLLM serves a known-good LoRA adapter and produces correct output (regression test confirming TP+LoRA corruption is absent under PP=2)
    78→- [ ] PEFT + bitsandbytes QLoRA fine-tune runs 1 training step without error (confirming quantization toolchain is functional)
    79→
    80→### Risk Callouts
    81→
    82→> **Driver/CUDA version mismatch:** PyTorch nightly cu128 requires CUDA 12.8+. Mismatched driver and toolkit versions produce cryptic errors at import time or during the first CUDA operation. Verify `nvidia-smi` reports CUDA 12.8+ and that `torch.version.cuda` matches.
    83→
    84→> **vLLM build from source:** Depending on the vLLM release at execution time, pipeline-parallel-size 2 support may require building vLLM from source. Confirm the installed vLLM version supports PP=2 before running the serving validation step.
    85→
    86→### Success Criteria
    87→
    88→| Criterion | Type | Target |
    89→|-----------|------|--------|
    90→| Both GPUs recognized by CUDA | Checklist | Pass (both in `nvidia-smi`; `device_count() == 2`) |
    91→| PyTorch forward+backward pass without segfault | Checklist | Pass (both GPUs) |
    92→| vLLM PP=2 serving without crash | Checklist | Pass |
    93→| TP+LoRA corruption absent under PP=2 | Checklist | Pass (known-good adapter produces correct output) |
    94→| QLoRA 1-step fine-tune without error | Checklist | Pass |
    95→
    96→---
    97→
    98→## Phase 1: Core Hypothesis Validation (Kill-Switch Gate)
    99→
   100→**Depends on:** Phase 0 passes all success criteria.
   101→
   102→Phase 1 tests the central hypothesis empirically: can a Doc-to-LoRA hypernetwork encode coding trajectories into LoRA adapters that improve task performance over the base model? No infrastructure is built until this gate passes. The rationale for this sequencing is that the adapter registry, serving layer, and recursive agent loop are all contingent on the hypothesis holding — building them before validation would be premature optimization of infrastructure around an unvalidated core idea.
   103→
   104→### Why This Phase Comes Before Infrastructure
   105→
   106→The infrastructure-first instinct — build the registry, the serving layer, the agent loop, then test the hypothesis — is common and historically problematic. Building infrastructure before validating the core idea embeds assumptions into architecture that are difficult to reverse if the idea fails. The study of failed ML projects (RAND 2024) consistently identifies premature infrastructure investment as a compounding failure mode: teams that discover a hypothesis failure late have also accumulated technical debt in systems that depend on it.
   107→
   108→Rune's kill-switch gate is the operational expression of hypothesis-first ordering: Phase 2 through Phase 4 are real and detailed, but they are explicitly conditional. Passing Phase 1 is what makes them worth building.
   109→
   110→### Deliverables
   111→
   112→- [ ] Minimal Doc-to-LoRA hypernetwork trained on 50-100 coding trajectory pairs (one trajectory per task: task description, attempt sequence, final passing code)
   113→- [ ] Adapter quality evaluation on held-out HumanEval subset (20-30 tasks, 5 samples per task)
   114→- [ ] MLflow run documenting: Pass@1 vs baseline, training loss curve, adapter cosine diversity across training batch, `||ΔW||` norms
   115→- [ ] Written assessment: what passed, what failed, what was learned — regardless of whether the gate passes or fails
   116→
   117→### Kill-Switch
   118→
   119→> **Primary metric:** Pass@1 improvement of ≥ 5% on held-out HumanEval tasks (20-30 task subset) compared to Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct baseline with no adapter.
   120→>
   121→> **If the gate passes:** The hypothesis has empirical support — not proof, but support. Proceed to Phase 2. The architectural decisions made in Phases 2 through 4 are now worth acting on.
   122→>
   123→> **If the gate fails:** Stop and document what was learned. There is no predefined fallback strategy. The failure narrows the design space — it is a research finding, not a project failure. The specific failure mode (mode collapse, no adapter transfer, training instability, insufficient trajectory signal) determines what comes next. Prescribing a fallback now would be speculative.
   124→
   125→**Hardware note for Phase 1:** Run the baseline in bfloat16 — not QLoRA. This isolates the hypothesis variable (does Doc-to-LoRA on coding trajectories work?) from the quantization variable (does NF4 quantization degrade adapter quality?). QLoRA is introduced in Phase 2 after the bfloat16 baseline passes.
   126→
   127→### Secondary Diagnostic Signals
   128→
   129→These are tracked via MLflow and inform the written assessment, but do not gate the kill-switch decision:
   130→
   131→- Adapter cosine diversity > 0.1 across training batch (early signal for mode collapse — if adapters are clustering, the hypernetwork is collapsing to the mean)
   132→- Training loss converges and does not plateau in the first 5% of the budget (training is learning, not stuck)
   133→- `||ΔW||` is meaningfully nonzero (the adapter is affecting the base model's behavior, not being ignored)
   134→
   135→### Risk Callouts
   136→
   137→> **Hypernetwork mode collapse** (see [Risk Matrix](appendices/risk-matrix.md)): The hypernetwork may learn to produce near-identical adapters regardless of input trajectory — the degenerate solution. Diversity regularization in the training loss and monitoring of cosine diversity are the primary mitigations. If diversity collapses during Phase 1, the gate will fail (Pass@1 will not improve across different task types), but the diagnostic signals should identify the failure mode before the full evaluation.
   138→
   139→> **Training data quality:** Trajectories must be diverse in task type, failure mode, and correction pattern. A dataset of 50-100 nearly-identical trajectories (e.g., all variations on the same task) will produce mode collapse regardless of architecture. Verify trajectory diversity before training begins.
   140→
   141→### Success Criteria
   142→
   143→| Criterion | Type | Target |
   144→|-----------|------|--------|
   145→| Pass@1 improvement on held-out HumanEval subset | **Kill-switch metric** | ≥ 5% over baseline |
   146→| MLflow run with required metrics logged | Checklist | Pass |
   147→| Written assessment produced | Checklist | Pass |
   148→| Adapter cosine diversity monitored | Checklist | Pass (tracked; not a gate) |
   149→
   150→### Experiment Sketch
   151→
   152→**Dataset:** 50-100 real coding trajectory pairs from HumanEval or SWE-bench-lite. Each trajectory consists of: task description, attempt sequence (code + error messages + corrections), final passing code. Trajectories sourced from existing evaluation runs or synthetically generated via a prompted base model.
   153→
   154→**Baseline:** Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct with no adapter — raw model Pass@1 on the held-out task subset (5 samples per task, bfloat16, PP=2 serving).
   155→
   156→**Evaluation method:** Pass@1 on 20-30 held-out HumanEval tasks. Five samples per task. Tasks held out from the training trajectory corpus to test generalization, not memorization.
   157→
   158→**Expected range:** 5-15% improvement over baseline signals a real effect and passes the gate. Less than 5% = gate fails. Greater than 15% should be treated skeptically and checked against the secondary diagnostics for data leakage.
   159→
   160→**Tracking:** MLflow experiment with schema: `run_id`, `phase`, `adapter_id`, `pass_at_1`, `training_loss`, `adapter_cosine_diversity`, `delta_w_norm`. Gate decision recorded as an MLflow run note: `"Gate PASSED"` or `"Gate FAILED — reassessing"`.
   161→
   162→---
   163→
   164→## Phase 2: Adapter Library and Serving Infrastructure
   165→
   166→**Depends on:** Phase 1 kill-switch passes.
   167→
   168→Assuming Phase 1 validates the core hypothesis, Phase 2 builds the component foundation: the adapter registry, vLLM serving with dynamic LoRA loading, API extensions, and QLoRA integration. These components are the dependency roots of the [build order](appendices/build-order.md) — every subsequent phase depends on them.
   169→
   170→### Why This Phase Comes Here
   171→
   172→The adapter registry (`libs/adapter-registry`) is the foundation of the entire system: every component that stores or retrieves adapters depends on it. The vLLM lora-server (`services/lora-server`) unblocks all agent work and hypothesis testing. Building these before Phase 3 or Phase 4 would have been premature if Phase 1 had failed — infrastructure built around an unvalidated hypothesis is wasted work. With Phase 1 passing, these components are now justified.
   173→
   174→QLoRA is introduced in this phase (not Phase 1) to isolate variables. The Phase 1 baseline established that the hypernetwork approach works in bfloat16. Phase 2 adds quantization and verifies that the quality loss is acceptable (<10% Pass@1 degradation) — a distinct measurement from the core hypothesis.
   175→
   176→### Deliverables
   177→
   178→- [ ] `libs/adapter-registry`: SQLModel schema, write-once enforcement at the storage API level, `.safetensors` path resolution, adapter metadata queryable without loading weights into GPU memory
   179→- [ ] `services/lora-server`: vLLM Dockerfile, startup script (`PP=2, TP=1, --enable-lora`), dynamic LoRA loading via vLLM's adapter API, health check endpoint
   180→- [ ] `services/api-service` extensions: `/adapters` and `/sessions` routes, SQLModel tables, REST interface for adapter registry queries
   181→- [ ] QLoRA integration: bfloat16 baseline → NF4 QLoRA transition with quality comparison logged to MLflow
   182→
   183→### Risk Callouts
   184→
   185→> **Adapter composition interference** (see [Risk Matrix](appendices/risk-matrix.md)): Default to single-adapter retrieval at inference time. Multi-adapter composition (additive merging of heterogeneous LoRAs) is an optional future experiment, not the default architecture. The risk of interference in non-orthogonal weight subspaces is real; the single-adapter default avoids it.
   186→
   187→> **Catastrophic forgetting** (see [Risk Matrix](appendices/risk-matrix.md)): Write-once semantics must be enforced at the registry API level, not as a convention. No code path may overwrite an existing adapter. Adapters are indexed by session ID and timestamp — if a new adapter is produced for the same task, it is a new entry, not an update.
   188→
   189→### Success Criteria
   190→
   191→| Criterion | Type | Target |
   192→|-----------|------|--------|
   193→| Adapter registry stores and retrieves by session ID and metadata | Checklist | Pass |
   194→| Write-once semantics enforced (no overwrite code path exists) | Checklist | Pass |
   195→| vLLM lora-server starts and serves with dynamic LoRA loading | Checklist | Pass |
   196→| No `--tensor-parallel-size 2` flag anywhere in config | Checklist | Pass |
   197→| QLoRA Pass@1 vs bfloat16 baseline degradation | Metric | < 10% degradation (logged in MLflow) |
   198→
   199→### Experiment Sketch
   200→
   201→**Dataset:** Same held-out HumanEval subset used in Phase 1 (20-30 tasks, 5 samples per task).
   202→
   203→**Baseline:** Phase 1 bfloat16 Pass@1 (already logged in MLflow).
   204→
   205→**Evaluation method:** Run the same held-out tasks with the Phase 1 adapter loaded into the Phase 2 vLLM lora-server, served in NF4 QLoRA mode. Compare Pass@1 between bfloat16 (Phase 1) and NF4 QLoRA (Phase 2).
   206→
   207→**Expected range:** < 10% degradation is acceptable and consistent with QLoRA paper results. Greater than 10% suggests quantization artifacts beyond expected range — investigate NF4 configuration before proceeding.
   208→
   209→---
   210→
   211→## Phase 3: Recursive Agent Loop and Sandbox Integration
   212→
   213→**Depends on:** Phase 2 success criteria met.
   214→
   215→Contingent on Phase 2 delivering a functional adapter registry and serving layer, Phase 3 builds the core agent loop (`services/rune-agent`) and the sandboxed code execution environment. This phase produces the first end-to-end path from task to adapter — the complete recursive loop described in the architecture.
   216→
   217→### Why This Phase Comes Here
   218→
   219→Phase 3 depends on Phase 2 at three integration points: the agent needs the adapter registry to select adapters at session start, the lora-server to load and serve them, and the api-service extensions to query and store session state. Without Phase 2, the agent loop has nowhere to retrieve or store adapters. Building the agent loop before the serving infrastructure would require mocking the entire adapter layer — wasted work that needs to be undone.
   220→
   221→Phase 3 also produces the adapter corpus required by Phase 4. The hypernetwork training job requires 50-100 diverse task-adapter pairs. The recursive agent loop is the mechanism that generates these pairs at scale. Phase 4 cannot begin until Phase 3 has produced sufficient corpus.
   222→
   223→### Deliverables
   224→
   225→- [ ] `services/rune-agent`: LangGraph `StateGraph` implementing `generate → execute → reflect → save` cycle, with configurable maximum attempt count
   226→- [ ] Sandbox: Docker-based code execution with network isolation, memory limits, and CPU limits; agent operates outside the container
   227→- [ ] Adapter selection: query adapter-registry at session start, load most-relevant adapter into lora-server based on task metadata
   228→- [ ] `libs/model-training` extensions: PEFT utilities, trajectory-to-adapter fine-tuning script (direct LoRA fine-tuning path, distinct from hypernetwork inference)
   229→- [ ] End-to-end test: task → agent loop → successful code → trajectory captured → passed to distillation → adapter stored in registry
   230→
   231→### Risk Callouts
   232→
   233→> **Sandbox escape:** Agent-generated code must not be able to reach the host network, host filesystem (outside the designated output directory), or other containers. Network isolation and read-only mounts are required from the first implementation — not added later as a hardening step.
   234→
   235→> **Agent loop divergence:** The generate-execute-reflect cycle requires a maximum attempt count. Without a hard stop, the loop retries indefinitely on tasks that are outside the model's current capability. The trajectory is still captured on loop termination (even without a passing solution) — a failed-but-attempted trajectory may still produce a useful adapter.
   236→
   237→### Success Criteria
   238→
   239→| Criterion | Type | Target |
   240→|-----------|------|--------|
   241→| Agent loop completes generate → execute → reflect → save cycle | Checklist | Pass |
   242→| Sandbox network isolation verified | Checklist | Pass (no outbound connections from container) |
   243→| Adapter selection queries registry and loads adapter | Checklist | Pass |
   244→| End-to-end test passes (task → adapter stored in registry) | Checklist | Pass |
   245→| Trajectory-to-adapter fine-tuning script produces loadable adapter | Checklist | Pass |
   246→
   247→---
   248→
   249→## Phase 4: Evolution Operator and Hypernetwork
   250→
   251→**Depends on:** Phase 3 success criteria met AND adapter corpus of 50-100 diverse task-adapter pairs accumulated from Phase 3 runs.
   252→
   253→Contingent on Phase 3 delivering a functional recursive agent loop, Phase 4 builds the adapter lifecycle management system (`services/evolution-svc`) and the Doc-to-LoRA hypernetwork inference path (`services/training-svc` hypernetwork job). This is the final phase and closes the loop: adapters produced by Phase 3 train the hypernetwork that generates future adapters.
   254→
   255→### Why This Phase Comes Last
   256→
   257→The hypernetwork requires a corpus of pre-trained adapters as training data — a cold-start problem that cannot be bypassed. Without Phase 3 producing diverse task-adapter pairs, the hypernetwork has nothing to train on. The evolution operator (`services/evolution-svc`) also depends on a populated adapter registry: fitness evaluation requires existing adapters to compare and promote.
   258→
   259→Attempting to build Phase 4 before Phase 3 is complete would require synthetic adapter data, which may not reflect the distribution of real coding task adapters. The ordering is forced by the data dependency.
   260→
   261→### Deliverables
   262→
   263→- [ ] `services/evolution-svc`: fitness evaluation against held-out test sets, tournament selection, adapter pruning below fitness threshold, promotion of high-performing adapters in the hierarchy
   264→- [ ] `services/training-svc`: hypernetwork training job (trains on Phase 3 adapter corpus), hypernetwork inference path (single forward pass → adapter weights, without gradient descent)
   265→- [ ] Adapter hierarchy: project-root, domain, and task-specific levels populated by the evolution operator from Phase 3 adapters
   266→- [ ] MLflow tracking: adapter fitness scores per evaluation run, evolution events (promotions, prunings, merges), hypernetwork reconstruction loss on held-out adapters
   267→
   268→### Risk Callouts
   269→
   270→> **Hypernetwork mode collapse** (see [Risk Matrix](appendices/risk-matrix.md)): Diversity regularization must be in the training loss from the start of hypernetwork training. Monitor adapter cosine diversity at each checkpoint — if it falls below the threshold (< 0.1), stop training and investigate. The Phase 1 experiment will have provided a reference baseline for what healthy cosine diversity looks like.
   271→
   272→> **Minimum corpus size:** The hypernetwork training requires a diverse adapter corpus. Diversity here is over task types, failure modes, and correction patterns — not just adapter count. If the Phase 3 corpus lacks sufficient diversity (e.g., all adapters trained on similar tasks), delay hypernetwork training and continue accumulating adapters from a wider task distribution. The Phase 3 end-to-end test verifies individual adapters; this is a separate concern about corpus-level diversity.
   273→
   274→### Success Criteria
   275→
   276→| Criterion | Type | Target |
   277→|-----------|------|--------|
   278→| Hypernetwork reconstruction loss on held-out adapters | Metric | Below baseline (random adapter) |
   279→| Adapter cosine diversity on hypernetwork outputs | Metric | > 0.1 threshold |
   280→| Evolution operator promotes, prunes, archives without corrupting registry | Checklist | Pass |
   281→| Hypernetwork-generated adapters load and run in vLLM without error | Checklist | Pass |
   282→| Hypernetwork-generated adapter Pass@1 vs direct fine-tuned adapter Pass@1 | Metric | Logged in MLflow (directional comparison, not a gate) |
   283→
   284→### Experiment Sketch
   285→
   286→**Dataset:** Held-out adapter subset from Phase 3 corpus (10-20% withheld from hypernetwork training set).
   287→
   288→**Baseline:** Random adapter (Gaussian weight initialization at the same rank) as reconstruction loss reference; direct fine-tuned adapter Pass@1 as inference quality reference.
   289→
   290→**Evaluation method:** Reconstruction loss (MSE between hypernetwork-generated adapter weights and held-out fine-tuned adapter weights); cosine diversity across a batch of hypernetwork-generated adapters; Pass@1 comparison on held-out HumanEval tasks using hypernetwork-generated vs fine-tuned adapters.
   291→
   292→**Expected range:** Reconstruction loss below random baseline confirms the hypernetwork is learning the adapter manifold. Cosine diversity > 0.1 confirms diversity is preserved. Pass@1 parity with fine-tuned adapters (±5%) would be a strong result; 50-80% of fine-tuned adapter quality is the expected range for a first-pass hypernetwork.

     1→# Rune
     2→
     3→SoTA-level coding performance from a local SLM, achieved by encoding experience into weight-space memory.
     4→
     5→![Research Stage](https://img.shields.io/badge/stage-research-orange)
     6→
     7→---
     8→
     9→## Abstract
    10→
    11→Current coding agents are bounded by context windows: each session begins fresh, and accumulated procedural knowledge — debugging patterns, project conventions, execution feedback — evaporates when the window closes. Rune hypothesizes that LoRA weight space can serve as persistent episodic memory, encoding what an agent has learned directly into the model's parameters rather than into tokens. The approach centers on a Doc-to-LoRA hypernetwork that converts coding trajectories into composable LoRA adapters in a single forward pass, combined with recursive distillation and a hierarchical adapter library that grows with each solved task. Rune is at the research stage: the architecture is documented, the component design is grounded in published work, and no implementation exists yet — the core hypothesis awaits empirical validation.
    12→
    13→---
    14→
    15→## Motivation
    16→
    17→Every coding agent that operates through in-context prompting faces the same ceiling: the context window. Inject enough code, tests, error messages, and documentation to be genuinely useful, and you exhaust the window. The only alternatives are truncation (losing history) or expensive retrieval (finding relevant text, not learned procedures). Neither addresses the underlying issue. Truncation discards context that was hard to produce. Retrieval adds latency and retrieves documents, not competence.
    18→
    19→Retrieval-augmented generation partially mitigates the problem by locating relevant documents at query time. But retrieval finds text that describes how something works — it does not encode the procedural knowledge of having done it. A senior developer does not need to retrieve documentation each time they fix a null pointer exception in a pattern they have resolved a hundred times before. That knowledge lives in their mental model, not in a document index. The difference is between declarative memory (knowing that something is true) and procedural memory (knowing how to do something). Current retrieval systems optimize for the former.
    20→
    21→Rune proposes a different substrate for memory: model weights. A LoRA adapter is a pair of low-rank matrices that additively shift the behavior of a frozen base model without modifying it. If a coding trajectory — the sequence of code attempts, execution results, errors, and corrections that led to a working solution — can be compressed into a LoRA adapter, then that experience becomes reusable across sessions, composable with other experiences, and independent of context window size. The parametric memory hypothesis is that this compression is possible and that the resulting adapters transfer meaningfully to similar future tasks.
    22→
    23→The practical consequence, if the hypothesis holds, is that a Small Language Model running locally on consumer hardware could accumulate coding competence over time rather than forgetting it between sessions. Each task solved makes the system marginally better at the next similar task. The adapter library grows. The quality of code generated for familiar patterns improves. This is qualitatively different from scaling context — it is the model updating its behavior in a targeted, reversible, composable way.
    24→
    25→---
    26→
    27→## Approach
    28→
    29→Rune's core mechanism is a Doc-to-LoRA hypernetwork [1] adapted for coding trajectories. The original Doc-to-LoRA work from Sakana AI demonstrates that a Perceiver-style encoder can map an input document directly to LoRA weight matrices via a single forward pass — approximately distilling the document into the adapter without gradient descent at inference time. Rune extends this in three directions:
    30→
    31→**1. Procedural knowledge encoding.** Doc-to-LoRA was validated on factual recall and needle-in-a-haystack tasks. Coding trajectories have a different structure: they are sequences of attempts, failures, error messages, and corrections. Rune proposes to train the hypernetwork on this trajectory format, encoding not just what to do but the corrective reasoning that led there. This is a qualitatively different input modality — whether the same Perceiver-style architecture handles it without modification is the first open question.
    32→
    33→**2. Recursive refinement.** The original Doc-to-LoRA is one-shot — a single forward pass over a document produces the adapter. Rune's agent generates code, executes it in a sandbox, observes the result, and iterates. The trajectory grows richer with each attempt before distillation. The hypothesis is that richer trajectories produce higher-quality adapters that generalize better — that the correction steps are signal, not noise.
    34→
    35→**3. Compositional memory through the Evolution Operator.** Doc-to-LoRA produces a single adapter intended to replace context for a given document. Rune builds a library: each solved task produces an adapter, and a hierarchical composition mechanism (the Evolution Operator) allows adapters to be merged, pruned, and promoted based on empirical fitness scores. Memory accumulates and compounds rather than being replaced.
    36→
    37→The weight update for a single LoRA adapter follows `ΔW = BA`, where `B` and `A` are low-rank matrices (rank `r << d`). This structure makes adapters parameter-efficient: at rank 64 on a 7B model, a full set of adapter weights is approximately 50-200 MB depending on which weight matrices are targeted. This is small enough to store, version, and load hundreds of adapters without approaching filesystem or VRAM limits.
    38→
    39→---
    40→
    41→## Architecture Overview
    42→
    43→Rune's architecture consists of three interacting components: the recursive code generation loop, the adapter hierarchy, and the serving layer.
    44→
    45→### The Recursive Loop
    46→
    47→The agent begins with a task and a set of candidate adapters selected from the adapter library. It generates code, executes it in an isolated sandbox, and evaluates the result. If tests fail, the trajectory is fed back into the generation step. When tests pass — or after a maximum attempt count — the complete trajectory is distilled into a new LoRA adapter by the Doc-to-LoRA hypernetwork, and that adapter is composed into the library.
    48→
    49→```mermaid
    50→flowchart LR
    51→    Task([Task]) --> Generate[Generate Code]
    52→    Generate --> Execute[Execute in Sandbox]
    53→    Execute --> Reflect{Tests Pass?}
    54→    Reflect -->|no| Generate
    55→    Reflect -->|yes| Distill[Distill Trajectory]
    56→    Distill --> HyperNet[Doc-to-LoRA\nHypernetwork]
    57→    HyperNet --> NewAdapter[(New LoRA\nAdapter)]
    58→    NewAdapter --> Compose[Compose with\nAdapter Library]
    59→    Compose --> Done([Task Complete])
    60→```
    61→
    62→The three Rune extensions to Doc-to-LoRA are visible in this loop: procedural trajectories enter the hypernetwork (not factual documents), the generate-execute-reflect cycle produces recursive refinement before distillation, and the Compose step merges the new adapter with the existing library rather than replacing it. The sandbox is network-isolated and resource-constrained — agent-generated code cannot escape the container.
    63→
    64→### The Adapter Hierarchy
    65→
    66→Adapters are organized in a three-level hierarchy: a project root adapter encodes high-level conventions and patterns, domain adapters encode task-type knowledge (async Python patterns, FastAPI idioms), and task-specific adapters encode solutions to individual problems. When a new task arrives, the adapter router selects the most relevant adapters at each level and loads them into the serving layer.
    67→
    68→```mermaid
    69→flowchart TD
    70→    Project[Project Root Adapter\ne.g. rune/main] --> Domain1[Domain: Python Async]
    71→    Project --> Domain2[Domain: FastAPI Patterns]
    72→    Domain1 --> Task1[Bug Fix #123]
    73→    Domain1 --> Task2[Bug Fix #456]
    74→    Domain2 --> Task3[Feature: OAuth]
    75→    Domain2 --> Task4[Feature: Rate Limiting]
    76→```
    77→
    78→The Evolution Operator manages this hierarchy: periodically evaluating adapter fitness on held-out tests, promoting high-performing adapters upward in the hierarchy, pruning low-performing ones, and merging adapters that have overlapping coverage. This lifecycle means the adapter library improves continuously as the agent works on more tasks. Adapters are stored as versioned `.safetensors` files on the local filesystem with metadata in SQLite; the registry is queryable without loading weights into GPU memory.
    79→
    80→### The Serving Architecture
    81→
    82→The base Small Language Model (SLM) runs in a vLLM server configured for pipeline parallelism across two GPUs. The adapter router queries the adapter registry — a SQLite metadata store — selects the relevant adapters for the current task, and loads them dynamically into the vLLM serving process. This design follows S-LoRA's unified paging approach [2], which manages adapter weights and KV cache tensors in a shared GPU memory pool, enabling concurrent serving of many adapters from a single base model without reloading weights.
    83→
    84→```mermaid
    85→flowchart LR
    86→    Request([Coding Request]) --> Router[Adapter Router]
    87→    Registry[(Adapter Registry\nSQLite + Filesystem)] --> Router
    88→    Router --> Server[vLLM Server\nPP=2]
    89→    BaseModel[Base SLM\nQwen2.5-Coder-7B] --> Server
    90→    Server --> Response([Generated Code])
    91→```
    92→
    93→The serving layer is intentionally separated from training: when the hypernetwork or fine-tuning jobs require GPU resources, the serving process yields GPUs via a lease mechanism rather than competing for VRAM. Pipeline parallelism splits the model layers across both GPUs and passes activations at layer boundaries — the correct strategy for GPUs connected via PCIe rather than NVLink.
    94→
    95→---
    96→
    97→## Theoretical Grounding
    98→
    99→Rune's architecture is a synthesis of three published approaches, extended for the coding agent setting.
   100→
   101→**Doc-to-LoRA** [1] is the central component. Sakana AI's hypernetwork maps input documents to LoRA weight matrices via a Perceiver-style encoder, achieving near-perfect needle-in-a-haystack accuracy at 4x the base model's native context window without any inference-time gradient descent. The approach is framed as "approximate context distillation" — the hypernetwork learns to compress a document's information into a weight delta that causes the base model to behave as if it had read the document. The key limitation for Rune's purposes is that Doc-to-LoRA was validated on factual recall — documents that state facts — rather than on procedural, trajectory-structured inputs. Rune's primary research question is whether the hypernetwork approach transfers to coding trajectories, and whether the three extensions (procedural encoding, recursive refinement, compositional memory) are necessary for that transfer to be useful.
   102→
   103→**S-LoRA** [2] addresses the serving challenge: a single base model must efficiently serve many different LoRA adapters concurrently, without loading and unloading adapters between requests. S-LoRA's Unified Paging mechanism manages adapter weights alongside KV cache tensors in a single GPU memory pool, and custom CUDA kernels handle heterogeneous batch LoRA computation — computing different adapter transforms for different items in the same batch. S-LoRA demonstrated "orders of magnitude" more concurrent adapters per GPU than naive PEFT loading. These techniques have been absorbed into vLLM's adapter serving infrastructure, which Rune uses directly rather than implementing from scratch.
   104→
   105→**QLoRA** [3] addresses the training constraint imposed by 24 GB per-GPU VRAM. By quantizing the base model to 4-bit NF4 and backpropagating gradients through the frozen quantized weights into bf16 LoRA adapters, QLoRA demonstrated fine-tuning of 65B models on a single consumer GPU with minimal quality loss. For Rune, QLoRA is essential: without it, a 7B base model in bf16 (~14 GB) leaves insufficient headroom for adapter weights, optimizer states, and activation memory on a 24 GB GPU during training. The NF4 data type (which is information-theoretically optimal for normally distributed weights) and double quantization (which quantizes the quantization constants themselves) are not optional — they are required for the hardware configuration to be viable.
   106→
   107→---
   108→
   109→## Design Principles
   110→
   111→- **Local-first.** Rune runs entirely on local hardware. No cloud API dependencies for inference, training, or adapter storage. Your data does not leave your machine.
   112→- **Empirically grounded.** Every architectural choice traces to a published result. When the hypothesis fails, the failure is informative — it narrows the design space for the field.
   113→- **Compositional memory.** Adapters accumulate and compose hierarchically rather than replacing each other. Experience compounds.
   114→- **Security-aware.** Agent-generated code executes in sandboxed containers with no network access and strict resource limits. The agent operates outside the sandbox.
   115→- **Transparent.** All adapter metadata is queryable: what tasks produced it, what fitness score it holds, what base model it targets. No black-box memory.
   116→- **Sovereign AI.** Your models, your weights, your hardware. The adapter library is yours and stored locally.
   117→
   118→---
   119→
   120→## Hardware Requirements
   121→
   122→Rune targets the following local hardware configuration:
   123→
   124→| Component | Specification |
   125→|-----------|--------------|
   126→| GPU | 2x NVIDIA RTX 4090 (24 GB VRAM each, 48 GB total) |
   127→| GPU Interconnect | CXL (cache-coherent memory pooling) |
   128→| CPU | AMD Threadripper 7960X |
   129→| CUDA | 12.8+ (cu128) |
   130→| PyTorch | 2.9+ (nightly, cu128 wheels) |
   131→| Quantization | QLoRA (NF4 4-bit) — required for 7B+ models on 24 GB |
   132→
   133→A single RTX 4090 is sufficient to evaluate inference-only workloads. Simultaneously training the hypernetwork and serving adapters requires both GPUs. Pipeline parallelism (`--pipeline-parallel-size 2`, `--tensor-parallel-size 1`) is the required multi-GPU configuration: the RTX 4090 lacks NVLink, and tensor parallelism requires all-reduce operations at every transformer layer — prohibitively expensive over a PCIe interconnect. CXL provides cache-coherent memory pooling across the two GPUs, which is relevant for the adapter registry and coordination between serving and training processes.
   134→
   135→Hardware validation is the first project milestone: before any hypothesis testing, both GPUs must be recognized by CUDA, PyTorch nightly cu128 must complete a forward and backward pass without segfault, and vLLM must serve the base model via pipeline parallelism without tensor parallelism corruption.
   136→
   137→Note on tensor parallelism: the `--tensor-parallel-size 2` option is explicitly excluded. Tensor parallelism requires all-reduce operations across GPUs at every transformer layer boundary. Without NVLink or a high-bandwidth interconnect, this becomes a severe bottleneck over PCIe (~32 GB/s vs NVLink's ~112 GB/s per direction) and can cause NCCL errors or OOM failures. Pipeline parallelism is the correct choice for this hardware configuration.
   138→
   139→---
   140→
   141→## Current Status
   142→
   143→**Stage:** Research / Pre-implementation
   144→
   145→Rune is a documented architecture proposal, not a working system. As of 2026-03-02:
   146→
   147→- No implementation exists
   148→- The core hypothesis — that Doc-to-LoRA can encode coding trajectories into reusable LoRA adapters — has not been empirically validated
   149→- The architecture synthesizes prior work (Doc-to-LoRA, S-LoRA, QLoRA) but adapter composition has not been demonstrated for coding tasks
   150→
   151→The project is structured so that early phases validate the hypothesis before infrastructure is built. Phase 0 validates the hardware environment and confirms vLLM pipeline parallelism works correctly. Phase 1 tests the core hypothesis with a measurable gate: if the Doc-to-LoRA approach does not produce adapters that improve Pass@1 on held-out coding tasks by at least 5%, the approach is revised before the serving infrastructure is built. If the hypothesis fails, the architecture documentation still stands as a concrete proposal that others can test, extend, or refute.
   152→
   153→The architecture is detailed enough to implement. The open question is whether the hypothesis holds.
   154→
   155→---
   156→
   157→## Open Questions
   158→
   159→- **Can Doc-to-LoRA encode procedural coding knowledge?** The hypernetwork was validated on factual recall. Coding trajectories have a different structure — sequential attempts, error messages, corrections. Does the same Perceiver-style architecture generalize to this input format, or does it require architectural modifications to handle trajectory-shaped inputs?
   160→- **Does recursive refinement improve adapter quality?** The baseline is one-shot distillation: a single forward pass over a complete trajectory. Does the iterative generate-execute-reflect loop produce richer trajectories that yield measurably better adapters, or is the marginal improvement small enough that one-shot is sufficient?
   161→- **How do composed adapters interact?** LoRA adapters for different tasks operate in different subspaces of the weight matrix. When composed additively, do they interact constructively (useful transfer across task types) or destructively (interference that degrades performance on both tasks)? The answer depends on how correlated the task distributions are and how the adapter ranks are chosen.
   162→- **What is the minimum adapter corpus size for hypernetwork training?** The hypernetwork requires a diverse corpus of pre-trained LoRA adapters as training data — a cold-start problem. How many adapters are needed before the hypernetwork produces useful outputs? This determines the feasibility timeline for the hypernetwork component specifically.
   163→
   164→---
   165→
   166→## References
   167→
   168→[1] Charakorn et al., "Doc-to-LoRA: Learning to Instantly Internalize Contexts," arXiv:2602.15902, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15902
   169→
   170→[2] Sheng et al., "S-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters," arXiv:2311.03285, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03285
   171→
   172→[3] Dettmers et al., "QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs," arXiv:2305.14314, 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314
   173→
   174→---
   175→
   176→## System Components
   177→
   178→Rune is structured as a monorepo with four new services and two extended libraries:
   179→
   180→| Component | Status | Role |
   181→|-----------|--------|------|
   182→| `services/rune-agent` | New | Recursive code generation loop (LangGraph), sandbox tool integration, adapter selection |
   183→| `services/lora-server` | New | vLLM subprocess serving base model with dynamic LoRA adapter loading |
   184→| `services/training-svc` | New | Async hypernetwork training and LoRA fine-tuning jobs |
   185→| `services/evolution-svc` | New | Adapter fitness evaluation, lifecycle management, pruning, and promotion |
   186→| `libs/adapter-registry` | New | Adapter metadata (SQLite), versioned `.safetensors` files on local filesystem |
   187→| `libs/model-training` | Extend | PEFT utilities, hypernetwork model definition |
   188→| `services/api-service` | Extend | REST API adding session and adapter registry routes |
   189→
   190→The build order follows component dependencies: `adapter-registry` first (no dependencies), then `lora-server` (unblocks all agent work), then `model-training` extensions, `api-service` extensions, `rune-agent`, `evolution-svc`, `training-svc`, and finally the hypernetwork (requires a corpus of pre-trained adapters). This ordering ensures the core hypothesis can be tested — with direct LoRA fine-tuning — before the hypernetwork component is built.
   191→
   192→---
   193→
   194→## Collaboration
   195→
   196→Rune is at the research stage — there is no working code to contribute to yet. But if you are working on hypernetwork training for procedural knowledge, LoRA episodic memory for agents, or local inference and training infrastructure on consumer hardware, this is adjacent territory. Discussion, critique, and related work are welcome.
   197→
   198→Open a thread in [GitHub Discussions](../../discussions) or reach out directly. The architecture is documented in detail in `.planning/` — the design decisions, hardware constraints, and open questions are all available for review.
   199→
   200→The most useful form of collaboration at this stage is critique: identifying flaws in the architectural reasoning, pointing to prior work that addresses the open questions, or sharing results from related experiments. Code contributions will become relevant once the core hypothesis is validated and implementation begins.
   201→

     1→# ElixirTrials  - Project Overview
     2→
     3→This document provides a comprehensive overview of the **ElixirTrials ** repository, its architecture, components, and development workflows.
     4→
     5→---
     6→
     7→## 🚀 Quick Start
     8→
     9→### Prerequisites
    10→- **Python 3.12+**
    11→- **Node.js 20+**
    12→- **uv** (Modern Python package manager)
    13→- **Docker & Docker Compose**
    14→
    15→### Installation
    16→Clone the repository and sync dependencies:
    17→
    18→```bash
    19→# Sync Python dependencies using uv
    20→uv sync
    21→
    22→# Install frontend dependencies
    23→cd apps/hitl-ui && npm install && cd ../..
    24→```
    25→
    26→---
    27→
    28→## 🏗️ System Architecture
    29→
    30→The project is a mono-repo combining Python backend services, LangGraph AI agents, and a React/Vite Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) frontend into a unified, high-performance architecture.
    31→
    32→### LangGraph Architecture
    33→The system follows a layered architecture:
    34→- **Presentation Layer**: React frontend (HITL UI)
    35→- **Application Layer**: FastAPI (API Service) + LangGraph Agents
    36→- **Data Layer**: Context Store, Message History
    37→- **Shared Layer**: Inference Service, Model Registry, Tool Registry
    38→
    39→```mermaid
    40→graph TB
    41→    subgraph Presentation["🎨 Presentation Layer"]
    42→        AdminUI[Admin Console UI]
    43→        HostDash[Host Dashboard]
    44→        GuestPanel[Guest Conversation Panel]
    45→        OrchPanel[System Orchestration Panel]
    46→    end
    47→
    48→    subgraph Application["⚙️ Application Layer"]
    49→        API[API Service]
    50→        ConvAgent[Conversation Agent]
    51→        GuardAgent[Guardrail Agent]
    52→        EventStream[Event Stream Service]
    53→    end
    54→
    55→    subgraph Data["💾 Data Layer"]
    56→        Context[(Context Store)]
    57→        History[(Message History)]
    58→        Signals[(Priority Signals)]
    59→    end
    60→
    61→    subgraph Shared["📦 Shared Components"]
    62→        Inference[Inference Service]
    63→        Models[Model Registry]
    64→        Tools[Tool Registry]
    65→    end
    66→
    67→    AdminUI --> HostDash
    68→    AdminUI --> GuestPanel
    69→    AdminUI --> OrchPanel
    70→
    71→    HostDash --> API
    72→    GuestPanel --> API
    73→    OrchPanel --> EventStream
    74→
    75→    API --> ConvAgent
    76→    API --> GuardAgent
    77→    ConvAgent --> Inference
    78→    GuardAgent --> Inference
    79→    ConvAgent --> Tools
    80→
    81→    EventStream --> ConvAgent
    82→    EventStream --> GuardAgent
    83→
    84→    ConvAgent --> Context
    85→    ConvAgent --> History
    86→    GuardAgent --> Signals
    87→
    88→    Inference --> Models
    89→
    90→    classDef presentation fill:#e1f5ff,stroke:#007acc,color:#000,stroke-width:2px;
    91→    classDef application fill:#d4f1d4,stroke:#28a745,color:#000,stroke-width:2px;
    92→    classDef data fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#ffc107,color:#000,stroke-width:2px;
    93→    classDef shared fill:#f0f0f0,stroke:#666,color:#000,stroke-width:2px;
    94→
    95→    class Presentation presentation;
    96→    class Application application;
    97→    class Data data;
