   112→### 1.3 Adapter Diversity Metrics
   113→
   114→**Source:** `implementation-plan.md` Phase 1 secondary diagnostic signals.
   115→
   116→These metrics do not gate the kill-switch decision but are tracked via MLflow and inform the post-experiment written assessment.
   117→
   118→#### \(\|\Delta W\|\) Norms
   119→
   120→The Frobenius norm of the adapter weight update \(\Delta W = BA\) for each generated adapter:
   121→
   122→\[
   123→\|\Delta W\|_F = \sqrt{\sum_{i,j} (\Delta W)_{ij}^2} = \|BA\|_F
   124→\]
   125→
   126→**Interpretation:** A meaningfully nonzero \(\|\Delta W\|_F\) confirms the adapter is affecting the base model's behavior. If \(\|\Delta W\|_F \approx 0\), the hypernetwork is generating near-zero updates — the adapter is effectively absent and provides no signal.
   127→
   128→**Per-layer reporting:** The article should note that \(\|\Delta W\|_F\) is reported per transformer layer targeted (Q, K, V, O projections and MLP up/down projections), giving a 6–8 dimensional profile rather than a single scalar.
   129→
   130→#### Cosine Similarity (Adapter Diversity)
   131→
   132→For a batch of hypernetwork-generated adapters \(\{\Delta W_i\}_{i=1}^{N}\), the inter-adapter cosine similarity is computed on flattened weight vectors:
   133→
   134→\[
   135→\text{sim}(i, j) = \frac{\text{vec}(\Delta W_i) \cdot \text{vec}(\Delta W_j)}{\|\text{vec}(\Delta W_i)\|_2 \cdot \|\text{vec}(\Delta W_j)\|_2}
   136→\]
   137→
   138→Mean pairwise cosine similarity across the batch is the diversity metric. The threshold from the implementation plan:
   139→
   140→- **Diversity criterion:** Mean pairwise cosine similarity < 0.9 (equivalently, adapter cosine diversity > 0.1)
   141→- **Interpretation:** If adapters are clustering (diversity collapses toward 0), the hypernetwork is approaching the degenerate "mean adapter" solution — a known mode collapse failure mode
   142→- **Source in risk matrix:** `docs/appendices/risk-matrix.md` — hypernetwork mode collapse warning sign: "Generated adapters cluster tightly in PCA; cosine similarity between adapters approaches 1.0"
   143→
   144→#### Table: Planned Experiment Metrics
   145→
   146→The article should present a table of all tracked metrics, clearly labeled:
   147→
   148→| Metric | Symbol | Threshold | Gate Type |
   149→|--------|--------|-----------|-----------|
   150→| Pass@1 improvement | — | ≥ 5% over baseline | **Kill-switch (primary gate)** |
   151→| Adapter \(\|\Delta W\|_F\) norm | \(\|\Delta W\|_F\) | Meaningfully nonzero | Diagnostic (not a gate) |
   152→| Inter-adapter cosine diversity | \(1 - \bar{\text{sim}}\) | > 0.1 | Diagnostic (not a gate) |
   153→| Training loss convergence | \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}\) | Converges, no early plateau | Diagnostic (not a gate) |
   154→
   155→Label: **Table 1 (Planned Experiments): Phase 1 Kill-Switch Evaluation Metrics**
   156→
   157→### 1.4 PBB-Inspired Evaluation Criterion
   158→
   159→**Source:** `instructions/some_new_insights.md`, Section 2 (Hypernetwork Training Objective).
   160→
   161→PBB (Cook et al., 2025) demonstrates that an LLM trained on source code without input-output examples can still evaluate those programs on new inputs — weight-based procedural encoding enables inference-time program execution. The specific test from the PBB methodology: given a program trained into weights via backpropagation, can the model evaluate that program on held-out inputs without those inputs in the context window?
   162→
   163→**Rune's adaptation:** The `some_new_insights.md` document explicitly prescribes:
   164→
   165→> Add a PBB-inspired objective: adapter should enable program evaluation without explicit I/O context
   166→> Test: generate adapter from code, evaluate on held-out inputs without those inputs in context window
   167→
   168→**Experimental description for the article:**
   169→
   170→A secondary evaluation criterion tests whether Rune's trajectory-conditioned adapters achieve the PBB property: can a generated adapter enable the model to evaluate a program on held-out inputs without those inputs appearing in the context window?
   171→
   172→The test procedure is:
   173→1. Generate an adapter from a trajectory that includes a specific algorithmic implementation (e.g., a sorting function, a string manipulation, a recursive algorithm)
   174→2. Load the adapter into the base model
   175→3. Query the model with a natural language request asking it to evaluate the function on held-out inputs — inputs not present in the training trajectory and not provided in context
   176→4. Compare: base model (no adapter) vs adapter-loaded model on the same held-out evaluation queries
   177→
   178→**Why this matters:** PBB's finding is that procedural knowledge can be encoded into weights such that the model can execute the procedure without in-context demonstration. If Rune's adapters achieve this property, it validates the weight-based procedural encoding hypothesis at a finer granularity than Pass@1 alone. Pass@1 measures whether the model can write passing code; the PBB criterion measures whether the model has internalized the algorithm itself.
   179→
   180→**Grounding:** The article must cite `[^cook2025pbb]` and note explicitly that PBB validated this criterion on a different task distribution (instruction-following with natural language programs) and that Rune proposes extending it to code execution trajectory-conditioned adapters.
   181→
   182→**Label:** Present as a subsection of Results, clearly marked "Proposed Evaluation Criterion (PBB-Inspired)" or included in a table labeled "Planned Experiments."
   183→
   184→### 1.5 Phase 4 Ablation Structure (Planned)

   188→**Ablation targets from Methods section:**
   189→- Encoder architecture: Perceiver-based cross-attention vs mean pooling vs hierarchical attention vs recurrent summarization
   190→- Fitness weight \(\alpha\): Default 0.7; ablation range TBD
   191→- Multi-adapter composition: Additive accumulation \(\Delta W_{\text{composite}} = \Delta W_{\text{project}} + \Delta W_{\text{domain}} + \Delta W_{\text{task}}\) vs single-adapter selection

   258→### 2.3 Expected Contributions Content
   259→
   260→Draw from Background and Methods to list the claimed contributions as "expected" or "proposed":
   261→
   262→1. **Trajectory modality extension (proposed):** Extending the hypernetwork-to-LoRA mechanism from document QA (Doc-to-LoRA) to code execution trajectories — a structurally distinct input modality with temporal ordering, procedural abstraction, and self-correcting structure. This is the central novel contribution claim.
   263→
   264→2. **Parametric episodic memory for coding agents (expected):** If the trajectory modality extension holds, Rune provides a composable weight-space memory alternative to context-window-based memory for long-running coding agents, directly addressing the limitation Pink et al. identify as the missing capability for long-term LLM agents.[^pink2025episodic]
   265→
   266→3. **Fitness-driven adapter lifecycle (specified):** The Evolution Operator's empirical fitness testing before adapter promotion, contrasted with LoRA Soups' assumption-based composition. This is specified in the architecture regardless of Phase 1 outcome.
   267→
   268→4. **PBB criterion validation for trajectory adapters (proposed):** If Rune's adapters satisfy the PBB program evaluation criterion, this extends Cook et al.'s finding from instruction-following to trajectory-conditioned weight-based procedural encoding.
   269→
   270→### 2.4 Limitations — Content Specifications
   271→
   272→**Source: risk matrix, implementation plan, and Background caveats.**
   273→
   274→#### Pre-Implementation Status
   275→The system has not been implemented. All architectural decisions are specified but untested at the component level. Phase 0 hardware validation (PP=2 + QLoRA + vLLM compatibility) has not been confirmed. The kill-switch gate outcome is unknown. Every "expected" claim depends on Phase 1 passing.
   276→
   277→The article should state this directly: "As of this writing, no training runs have been executed, no adapters have been generated, and no Pass@1 measurements have been taken. This article presents a research proposal, not a completed study."
   278→
   279→#### Adapter Interference Risk
   280→From Background (Zhang et al.[^zhang2025orthogonality] and Zou[^zou2026merging]): orthogonality between adapter subspaces does not guarantee semantic disentanglement. Additive composition of heterogeneous adapters can produce interference even in mathematically orthogonal subspaces, and can reactivate latent reasoning traces from individual adapters.
   281→
   282→Rune's default single-adapter retrieval mode mitigates this for the common case, but multi-adapter composition (the ablation target for Phase 5+) remains unvalidated. The Evolution Operator's fitness-driven selection is designed to detect interference empirically rather than prevent it theoretically — but this detection mechanism has not been tested.
   283→
   284→#### Hypernetwork Mode Collapse
   285→From the risk matrix: the hypernetwork may learn the degenerate solution — producing a near-identical "mean adapter" regardless of input trajectory. Diversity regularization in the training loss is the primary mitigation, but the correct regularization weight is unknown before training. The diversity threshold (cosine similarity < 0.9) is a heuristic, not a theoretically grounded bound.
   286→
   287→If mode collapse occurs in Phase 1, the kill-switch gate will fail — but the specific failure mode (loss converges, Pass@1 does not improve, adapters cluster in PCA) will provide information about the severity and whether targeted regularization can recover.
   288→
   289→#### Cold-Start Corpus Size
   290→The hypernetwork training (Phase 4) requires a corpus of pre-trained adapters from Phase 3. The minimum corpus size for useful hypernetwork training is unknown. The implementation plan sets a target of 50–100 diverse task-adapter pairs, but this is a heuristic estimate. Corpus diversity — over task types, failure modes, and correction patterns — matters more than raw count, but the minimum diversity level is also unknown.
   291→
   292→The cold-start problem is two-layered: first, enough trajectories to train Phase 3 direct LoRA adapters; second, enough Phase 3 adapters to train the Phase 4 hypernetwork. If early-phase trajectory collection produces insufficiently diverse corpora, both training stages will be degraded.
   293→
   294→### 2.5 Open Research Questions — Content Specifications
   295→
   296→**Source: ROADMAP success criterion 3 (four prescribed questions), Methods claim tiers, and Background open questions.**
   297→
   298→#### Procedural Encoding in Weight Space
   299→Can code execution trajectories be encoded into LoRA weight deltas such that the base model can execute the encoded procedure on novel inputs without those inputs in context? This is the PBB criterion applied to trajectories. Background establishes PBB's finding (instructions substitute for up to 100 examples); the question is whether trajectory-conditioned adapters close the gap between encoding efficiency and reliable weight-based execution that PBB identifies.
   300→
   301→The question has two levels: (a) does Pass@1 improve (the kill-switch); and (b) does the PBB program evaluation criterion hold (a stronger test). A system could pass (a) by improving solution generation without achieving (b).
   302→
   303→#### Recursive Refinement Value
   304→The generate-execute-reflect loop produces trajectories of variable depth (1 to `max_attempts` attempts). Does recursive refinement — multiple attempts with error feedback — produce substantially better adapters than single-attempt trajectories? If a successful first-attempt trajectory and a successful 5-attempt trajectory produce similar adapters, the recursive loop adds trajectory collection cost without improving adapter quality. If multi-attempt trajectories produce better adapters (because they contain failure-recovery patterns), the recursive loop is essential to the architecture.
   305→
   306→This question is not addressed by the Phase 1 kill-switch (which tests whether any trajectory-conditioned adapter improves Pass@1). It requires a controlled ablation: single-attempt vs multi-attempt trajectories, matched on task, compared on resulting adapter quality.
   307→
   308→#### Composition Interference
   309→At what point does multi-adapter composition (additive accumulation across hierarchy levels) degrade performance relative to single-adapter selection? Background documents the theoretical concern; Zhang et al.[^zhang2025orthogonality] show orthogonality is insufficient; Zou[^zou2026merging] shows latent trace reactivation. But no empirical measurement exists for Rune's specific adapter distribution.
   310→
   311→The question is not whether composition can interfere (it can) but at what combination depth and diversity level interference becomes the dominant effect. The Phase 5+ ablation target for multi-adapter composition is designed to answer this question empirically.
   312→
   313→#### Cold-Start Minimum
   314→What is the minimum corpus size (in terms of trajectory count and diversity) required to train a hypernetwork that generates useful adapters? The implementation plan uses 50–100 as a heuristic. The cold-start minimum determines the practical feasibility of the Phase 4 training approach and whether the Phase 3 accumulation rate is sufficient.
   315→
   316→### 2.6 Future Work — Content Specifications
   317→
   318→**Source: ROADMAP success criterion 3, `instructions/project_initialization.md` (QDoRA reference), implementation plan.**
   319→
   320→#### QDoRA Integration
   321→From `instructions/project_initialization.md`:
   322→
   323→> **QDoRA (Quantized Decomposed LoRA):** Decomposes weight updates into magnitude and direction. More closely mimics full fine-tuning dynamics. Faster convergence on complex reasoning tasks. Compatible with 4-bit quantization. Future enhancement for Evolution Operator.
   324→
   325→QDoRA is not in the current architecture — it is listed as a future enhancement. In the context of the Discussion, QDoRA integration would replace the QLoRA quantization baseline with a decomposed update scheme that potentially improves adapter quality during the Phase 3 direct LoRA bootstrapping stage. Whether QDoRA's convergence advantages transfer to short-horizon adapter training on coding trajectories is unknown.
   326→
   327→#### Cross-Project Transfer
   328→The three-level adapter hierarchy (project, domain, task) is designed to support transfer: domain-level adapters should capture patterns that generalize across projects. Whether domain-level adapters trained on one project's trajectories produce meaningful improvement on a different project's tasks is an open empirical question.
   329→
   330→Cross-project transfer testing would require: (a) accumulating adapters from at least two distinct projects; (b) evaluating domain-level adapters (trained on project A's trajectories) on tasks from project B; (c) comparing against project-specific and vanilla baselines.
   331→
   332→#### Online Adaptation
   333→The current architecture assumes a batch training paradigm: collect trajectories, train adapters offline, update the registry. Online adaptation would mean the hypernetwork updates continuously as new trajectories arrive, without discrete training runs. This would require streaming training infrastructure and a mechanism to prevent catastrophic forgetting in the hypernetwork itself (not just in the base model).
   334→
   335→Online adaptation is explicitly out of scope for the current implementation plan but is a natural extension if Phase 4 hypernetwork training proves stable.
   336→
   337→### 2.7 Broader Implications Content
   338→
   339→The Discussion should close with a brief subsection on broader implications, connecting Rune's design to the episodic memory position paper:
   340→
   341→- Pink et al.[^pink2025episodic] argue that episodic memory is the missing capability for long-term LLM agents. Rune's adapter-per-session design is one concrete instantiation of this position — each adapter is an episode, retrieved by task similarity, composable with other episodes.
   342→- The trajectory modality argument extends PBB's procedural encoding insight: if instructions are efficient training signal, trajectories — which contain both the procedure and its execution context — may be the most information-dense substrate available for weight-based procedural encoding.
   343→- The kill-switch gate structure is itself a methodological contribution: explicitly conditioning infrastructure investment on hypothesis validation before building the dependent components.
   344→

   377→## Architecture Patterns
   378→
   379→### Pattern 1: MkDocs Admonition for Status Disclaimers
   380→
   381→Established in the MkDocs infrastructure (Phase 8). Use for research-status framing:
   382→
   383→```markdown
   384→!!! warning "Research Status: Pre-Implementation"
   385→    No experiments have been conducted. This section presents the planned
   386→    experimental design for Phase 1 hypothesis validation. All tables, figures,
   387→    and metrics below describe proposed measurements, not observed results.
   388→```
   389→
   390→### Pattern 2: Claim-Tier Labeling
   391→
   392→From Methods section — every sentence with a performance verb must carry a tier label. In Results/Discussion, extend to cover the future-tense framing:
   393→
   394→| Phrase | Claim Tier |
   395→|--------|-----------|
   396→| "We expect that..." | expected |
   397→| "The proposed evaluation..." | proposed |
   398→| "The architecture specifies..." | specified |
   399→| "Prior work demonstrates..." | validated (cite the paper) |
   400→| "No experiments have confirmed..." | explicitly stated |
   401→
   402→### Pattern 3: "Planned Experiments" Table Labels
   403→
   404→Every table or figure in results.md must be labeled explicitly. Pattern:
   405→
   406→```markdown
   407→*Table N (Planned Experiments): [Description]*
   408→```
   409→
   410→or as a caption inside a block:
   411→
   412→```markdown
   413→/// caption
   414→Table N (Planned Experiments): [Description]
   415→///
   416→```
   417→
   418→### Pattern 4: Footnote Citation
   419→
   420→Established in Background and Methods. Use throughout:
   421→
   422→```markdown
   423→Cook et al. demonstrate that declarative instructions can substitute for up
   424→to 100 execution examples.[^cook2025pbb]
   425→```
   426→
   427→With footnote at section end:
   428→
   429→```markdown
   430→[^cook2025pbb]: Cook, J., et al. (2025). Programming by Backprop: An Instruction is Worth 100 Examples When Finetuning LLMs. *arXiv:2506.18777*. [Full entry](references.md#cook2025pbb)
   431→```

   435→## Don't Hand-Roll
   436→
   437→| Problem | Don't Build | Use Instead | Why |
   438→|---------|-------------|-------------|-----|
   439→| Research-status framing | Custom HTML disclaimer blocks | MkDocs `!!! warning` admonition | Consistent styling with rest of site; already configured in Phase 8 |
   440→| Math equations | Raw HTML MathML | `\(...\)` / `\[...\]` with MathJax (configured Phase 8) | Already working; tested in Methods section |
   441→| Citation footnotes | Inline reference lists | `[^citekey]` footnote syntax | Already working; tested in Background and Methods |
   442→| Section cross-references | External links | Relative Markdown links (`methods.md#evolution-operator`) | MkDocs resolves these correctly |

   445→
   446→## Common Pitfalls
   447→
   448→### Pitfall 1: Empirical Claims Without Qualification
   449→**What goes wrong:** Writing "Rune achieves X% improvement" or "the system reduces Y" without claim-tier qualification or explicit "Planned Experiments" label.
   450→**Why it happens:** Natural writing voice shifts to present tense when describing expected behavior.
   451→**How to avoid:** Every sentence in Results/Discussion containing a performance verb (achieves, improves, enables, demonstrates, reduces) must be prefixed with "We expect that..." or "The proposed design..." or cite prior work for validated claims.
   452→**Warning signs:** Present-tense sentences without citations or claim-tier labels.
   453→
   454→### Pitfall 2: Over-Qualifying to the Point of Vagueness
   455→**What goes wrong:** The "Planned Experiments" framing becomes a hedge that strips all specificity — thresholds become "some improvement," benchmarks become "standard evaluation," metrics become "various measures."
   456→**Why it happens:** Over-correction from the fear of making empirical claims.
   457→**How to avoid:** Use the exact numbers from the implementation plan. "≥ 5% Pass@1 improvement on a 20–30 task HumanEval subset" is a proposed threshold, not an empirical claim. Specificity is what makes the research proposal credible.
   458→**Warning signs:** Threshold ranges disappear; benchmark names are replaced by category descriptors.
   459→
   460→### Pitfall 3: Wrong Math Delimiters
   461→**What goes wrong:** Using `$...$` or `$$...$$` instead of `\(...\)` and `\[...\]`.
   462→**Why it happens:** Dollar-sign syntax is the default in most LaTeX editors and many Markdown guides.
   463→**How to avoid:** The MkDocs arithmatex extension is configured for `\(...\)` and `\[...\]` only. Dollar signs will not render.
   464→**Warning signs:** Equations appear as raw text in the built site.
   465→
   466→### Pitfall 4: Missing Footnote Declarations
   467→**What goes wrong:** `[^citekey]` reference used in body text but the corresponding `[^citekey]: ...` footnote declaration is absent or placed outside the file scope.
   468→**Why it happens:** Easy to write inline citations during drafting and add footnotes later, then miss some.
   469→**How to avoid:** Add each footnote declaration immediately after its first use in the body, or collect all at the end of the file (both work in MkDocs).
   470→**Warning signs:** MkDocs build warns about undefined footnote references.
   471→
   472→### Pitfall 5: Discussion Repeating Methods Content
   473→**What goes wrong:** Discussion re-explains the Evolution Operator, hypernetwork architecture, or recursive loop in detail.
   474→**Why it happens:** The Discussion author wants to remind the reader of relevant context.
   475→**How to avoid:** Cross-reference the Methods section with relative links: "as specified in the Evolution Operator section (see Methods)." Discussion adds interpretive commentary, it does not re-derive.
   476→**Warning signs:** Paragraphs beginning "Recall that the hypernetwork H: T → (B, A)..."
   477→
   478→---
   479→
   480→## Code Examples
   481→
   482→### Metric Equations for results.md
   483→
   484→**Pass@1 definition (standard formulation):**
   485→```markdown
   486→Pass@1 for a single task is the probability that the first generated sample
   487→passes all tests. Averaged over \(N\) tasks with \(k=5\) samples each:
   488→
   489→\[
   490→\text{Pass@1} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbb{1}[\text{task}_i \text{ passes on at least 1 of } k \text{ samples}]
   491→\]
   492→```
   493→
   494→**Frobenius norm equation:**
   495→```markdown
   496→\[
   497→\|\Delta W\|_F = \sqrt{\sum_{i,j} (B A)_{ij}^2}
   498→\]
   499→```
   500→
   501→**Cosine similarity between adapters:**
   502→```markdown
   503→\[
   504→\text{sim}(\Delta W_i, \Delta W_j) = \frac{\text{vec}(\Delta W_i) \cdot \text{vec}(\Delta W_j)}{\|\text{vec}(\Delta W_i)\|_2 \, \|\text{vec}(\Delta W_j)\|_2}
   505→\]
   506→```
   507→
   508→**Fitness function (from Methods, for reference in Discussion):**
   509→```markdown
   510→\[
   511→\phi(a) = \alpha \cdot \text{pass\_rate}(a) + (1 - \alpha) \cdot \text{generalization}(a), \quad \alpha = 0.7
   512→\]
   513→```

    35→### What background.md says
    36→
    37→- **Problem framing:** Local coding agents (Aider, Cursor, Claude Code) lose context between sessions — patterns, bugs solved, architectural decisions — because they operate in fixed context windows. Three memory categories exist: token-space (RAG), destructive weight-space (ROME/full fine-tuning), composable weight-space (LoRA adapters).
    38→- **Rune's position:** Composable weight-space. Each session produces a write-once LoRA adapter encoding procedural knowledge as parameter deltas.
    39→- **LoRA math:** `ΔW = BA` where rank r ≪ min(d,k). Adapter contribution is additive and reversible.
    40→- **QLoRA:** NF4 quantization brings 7B model from ~14 GB to ~4 GB — enables consumer GPU operation.
    41→- **S-LoRA:** Validates that thousands of concurrent adapters are servable from one base model instance (Unified Paging).
    42→- **Doc-to-LoRA:** Hypernetwork → LoRA in one forward pass, validated on document QA. NOT validated on code trajectories.
    43→- **SHINE:** Hypernetwork from in-context examples. Input: demonstration pairs. NOT trajectories.
    44→- **LoRA Soups CAT:** Binary skill composition can outperform data mixing — but orthogonality ≠ semantic disentanglement (Zhang et al.), and merging can reactivate latent traces (Zou).
    45→- **PBB:** Instructions substitute for up to 100 examples for fine-tuning — procedural representations are information-dense. BUT in-context execution remains more reliable than weight-based execution.
    46→- **Trajectory modality argument:** Code execution trajectories are structurally distinct from documents, examples, and instructions — temporal ordering, procedural abstraction, self-correcting structure (attempt → error → fix).
    47→
    48→### What methods.md says
    49→
    50→- **Five services:** rune-agent, lora-server, training-svc, evolution-svc, adapter-registry (SQLite + safetensors).
    51→- **Hypernetwork mapping:** `H: T → (B, A)` where T = trajectory space. Perceiver-based encoder produces fixed-size latent from variable-length trajectory. Per-layer output heads produce (B, A) pairs. This is **proposed** — the trajectory modality extension has not been validated.
    52→- **Distillation pipeline:** Phase 3 = direct LoRA fine-tuning (specified). Phase 4 = hypernetwork forward pass (proposed).
    53→- **Evolution Operator:** Consolidate/Update/Forget/Merge operations. Fitness function `φ(a) = α·pass_rate(a) + (1-α)·generalization(a)`, default α=0.7 (ablation target). Merge is an ablation target due to interference risk.
    54→- **Three-level hierarchy:** project/domain/task. Default = single-adapter selection (specified). Multi-adapter composition = ablation target.
    55→- **Serving:** vLLM PP=2 + QLoRA, intended configuration pending Phase 0 validation (not confirmed working).

    61→- **Four baselines:** vanilla model, RAG baseline, directly fine-tuned LoRA, hypernetwork-generated adapter.
    62→- **Diversity metrics:** Frobenius norm (diagnostic), inter-adapter cosine diversity > 0.1 (diagnostic).
    63→- **PBB criterion (proposed):** Can adapter enable model to evaluate function on held-out inputs without those inputs in context? Secondary criterion, not part of kill-switch.

If the cover page links to section pages using heading anchors (e.g., `abstract.md#abstract`), those headings must exist.
   354→
   355→3. **`unrecognized_links: warn`** — any malformed links. Use relative paths for intra-article links.
   356→
   357→4. **`absolute_links: warn`** — do not use absolute paths beginning with `/` for internal links.
   358→
   359→### Internal link convention
   360→
   361→All existing article files use relative paths for cross-section links:
   362→- `[Background](background.md)` — correct
   363→- `[Methods](methods.md#evolution-operator)` — correct (heading anchor)
   364→- `[Full entry](references.md#citekey)` — correct
   365→
   366→The new `abstract.md` and updated `index.md` must follow the same convention.
   367→
   368→### Heading anchor generation
   369→
   370→MkDocs generates heading anchors from the heading text. The heading `## Abstract` generates anchor `#abstract`. The heading `### Expected Contributions` generates `#expected-contributions`. When linking from the cover page TOC to section headings, use lowercase hyphenated forms:
   371→- `background.md#background` (section heading is `## Background`)
   372→- `methods.md#methods`
   373→- `results.md#results`
   374→- `discussion.md#discussion`
   375→
   376→---
   377→
   378→## File Specifications
   379→
   380→### docs/article/abstract.md
   381→
   382→**Structure:**
   383→
   384→```markdown
   385→## Abstract
   386→
   387→<div class="abstract" markdown="1">
   388→**Abstract.** [~250 word text with claim tiers]
   389→</div>
   390→```
   391→
   392→**No footnote definitions** — abstracts do not cite. No math. No admonitions.
   393→
   394→**Word count target:** 240-260 words in the abstract div.
   395→
   396→**Claim tier usage in the abstract text:**
   397→- "validated by Doc-to-LoRA" or "validated on document QA" — for the hypernetwork mechanism
   398→- "expected to" — for parametric episodic memory benefit (depends on Phase 1)
   399→- "proposed" — for the trajectory modality extension (central hypothesis)
   400→
   401→### docs/article/index.md (cover page rewrite)
   402→
   403→**Required elements:**
   404→1. `# Rune: Parametric Episodic Memory for Local Coding Agents` (or similar title)
   405→2. `.author-block` div with author name, year
   406→3. `!!! warning "Research Status: Pre-Implementation"` admonition
   407→4. Linked TOC as a markdown list
   408→5. Short one-paragraph description of the article (optional but recommended)
   409→
   410→**Remove from current index.md:**
   411→- "Rendering Test" section
   412→- Local `[^hu2021lora]` footnote definition (test artifact)
   413→- "Sections / The article will include:" stub list (replace with real linked TOC)
   414→- Placeholder abstract div with "Content forthcoming"
   415→
   416→**Linked TOC format:**
   417→```markdown
   418→- [Abstract](abstract.md)
   419→- [Background](background.md)
   420→- [Methods](methods.md)
   421→- [Results](results.md)
   422→- [Discussion](discussion.md)
   423→- [References](references.md)
   424→```
   425→
   426→---
   427→
   428→## Common Pitfalls
   429→
   430→### Pitfall 1: Claiming too much in the abstract
   431→
   432→**What goes wrong:** Abstract says "Rune improves Pass@1 by X%" or "Rune enables persistent memory" as if results exist.
   433→**Why it happens:** The roadmap goal text sounds affirmative; easy to slip into present tense.
   434→**How to avoid:** Every performance-related claim must use "proposed", "expected", or "if Phase 1 validates". The article's Results section is PLANNED experiments. The abstract must reflect this.
   435→**Warning signs:** Any sentence in the abstract without a claim-tier qualifier describing Rune's performance.
   436→
   437→### Pitfall 2: Abstract too long or too short
   438→
   439→**What goes wrong:** Writing a mini-paper introduction (400+ words) or a one-sentence pitch (50 words).
   440→**How to avoid:** Target 250 words exactly. Each of the four required elements (problem, approach, mechanism, contribution) gets one substantive paragraph or 2-3 sentences.
   441→
   442→### Pitfall 3: Forgetting the nav update when adding abstract.md
   443→
   444→**What goes wrong:** abstract.md created but not added to mkdocs.yml nav → `omitted_files: warn` → build gate fails.
   445→**How to avoid:** The nav update and file creation are the same atomic change in Plan 12-01.
   446→
   447→### Pitfall 4: Cover page index.md footnote duplication
   448→
   449→**What goes wrong:** Leaving `[^hu2021lora]` local definition in index.md while background.md also defines it → footnote numbering behaves correctly per MkDocs but the local definition lacks the `[Full entry]` link.
   450→**How to avoid:** Remove the test footnote from index.md entirely. The cover page should not cite papers.
   451→
   452→### Pitfall 5: Absolute links in the cover page TOC
   453→
   454→**What goes wrong:** Writing `[Abstract](/docs/article/abstract.md)` instead of `[Abstract](abstract.md)`.
   455→**Why it happens:** Habit from web development.
   456→**How to avoid:** All internal links use relative paths. `absolute_links: warn` is active.
   457→
   458→### Pitfall 6: Math delimiters in the abstract
   459→
   460→**What goes wrong:** Using `$E = mc^2$` style delimiters anywhere in abstract or index.
   461→**How to avoid:** The project uses ONLY `\(...\)` for inline math and `\[...\]` for block math. The abstract should have no math at all.
   462→

   468→- Direct inspection of `docs/article/background.md` — all content, citations, citekeys
